title: SpaceX Is About to Become the Largest IPO in History. The Number Is $1.75 Trillion.
excerpt: Elon Musk's rocket, satellite and AI conglomerate will raise at least $75 billion when it lists on the Nasdaq on June 12. Morningstar says the company is worth less than half that.
body:
SpaceX, the rocket and satellite company that has become the crown jewel of Elon Musk's business empire, confirmed on Tuesday that it is targeting a valuation of $1.75 trillion in what would be the largest initial public offering in history.

## The Numbers

The company plans to raise at least $75 billion through an all-primary offering on the Nasdaq, meaning every dollar raised will go to SpaceX rather than to existing shareholders. The roadshow begins on Thursday, June 4, with the stock expected to debut on June 12.

Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley, Bank of America, Citigroup and JPMorgan are leading the underwriting syndicate. SpaceX is negotiating fees of less than 0.75% on the raise — a fraction of typical IPO commissions — though the banks will still collect roughly $500 million from the deal, according to Bloomberg.

The IPO will give public investors their first chance to buy directly into the company that dominates commercial space launch, operates the Starlink satellite broadband network, and now houses Musk's artificial intelligence venture xAI and the social media platform X.

## A Contrarian Warning

Not everyone is buying the hype. Morningstar published its own valuation on Tuesday, pegging SpaceX at $780 billion — less than half the IPO target.

"We think the company has been significantly overvalued and investors will have opportunities to buy the stock at more attractive levels after the IPO," said Morningstar equity analyst Nicolas Owens. He flagged xAI's uncertain economics and competition from OpenAI and Anthropic, noting bluntly: "We don't see Grok as one of the leading AI labs today."

SpaceX carried about $30 billion in debt and $16 billion in cash as of the first quarter of 2026, with $20 billion of that debt in a bridge loan that matures 15 months after the IPO. The company is not yet profitable by traditional measures, a fact that critics say makes the $1.75 trillion valuation a bet on narrative rather than fundamentals.

## Why Markets Are Nervous

The sheer size of the IPO has Wall Street worried about its gravitational pull on the broader market. SpaceX is expected to be added to the S&P 500 almost immediately after listing, which would force every passive index fund in the world to buy shares.

"Every retail investor holding an S&P 500 ETF in their 401(k) would become an involuntary SpaceX shareholder, regardless of whether they believe in the story," said Jay Woods, chief strategist at Freedom Capital Markets. "The index wasn't designed to do that."

Harrison Rolfes at PitchBook called it the "most consequential IPO cycle since the dot-com era" — noting that SpaceX and Anthropic, which is also preparing to list, together represent the largest concentration of pre-IPO capital ever brought to public markets simultaneously.

## What It Means for India

The IPO carries several implications for Indian markets and the broader diaspora tech ecosystem. Indian-origin engineers form a significant portion of SpaceX's workforce, particularly in its Starlink and propulsion divisions. For Indian retail investors, who have increasingly looked to US markets through liberalised remittance and fractional-share platforms, the listing creates both opportunity and risk.

More strategically, SpaceX's public debut raises questions about India's own space economy. ISRO and a growing crop of Indian private space startups — including Skyroot Aerospace, Agnikul Cosmos and Pixxel — are building commercial capabilities, but none operate at SpaceX's scale. Starlink's pending application for broadband spectrum in India, which has been mired in regulatory debate since 2022, could receive fresh momentum if the IPO demonstrates overwhelming investor demand for satellite communications.

The listing also arrives at a moment when global capital markets are flush but anxious. The S&P 500 has gained more than 16% this quarter, and the tech-heavy Nasdaq nearly 25%. Some analysts warn that the SpaceX IPO could mark the top, as funds rotate out of liquid large-caps to make room for the new entrant.

For Indian investors tracking global tech, the message is clear: the era of space, satellite and AI convergence has arrived at public markets. Whether the price is right is another question entirely.
